facts.statehood_note: Oregon became the 33rd state on Valentine's Day, February 14, 1859, but the news did not reach Oregon until March 15.
facts.motto: Alis volat propriis (Latin for "She flies with her own wings"), adopted in 1987, replacing "The Union"
facts.name_origin: No one knows for sure. Ideas include a 1765 spelling "Ouragon" by Major Robert Rogers (possibly from the French word for windstorm), the Spanish word orejón ("big ears"), and a mapmaker's mistake on an old French map.

government.legislature: Oregon Legislative Assembly, which meets every year at the State Capitol in Salem (a 2010 vote of the people made yearly meetings the rule)
government.chambers: Oregon State Senate (30 senators, 4-year terms, half elected every two years) and Oregon House of Representatives (60 members, 2-year terms)
government.executive: Governor (4-year term; the governor may not serve more than eight years in any 12-year period). Oregon has no lieutenant governor: if the office is empty, the Secretary of State is next in line, then the State Treasurer.
government.courts: Oregon Supreme Court (7 justices, elected statewide to 6-year terms; they choose one of their own as Chief Justice). Below it are the Oregon Court of Appeals (13 judges since a 2012 law) and 36 circuit courts, the state's trial courts.
government.local: 36 counties, each led by a board of county commissioners, and 242 incorporated places (233 cities and 9 towns) as of 2010.
government.constitution: Written by leaders of Oregon Territory in 1857, approved by voters in November 1857, and in effect since statehood on February 14, 1859. The original version barred Black people from living in Oregon and kept Black and Chinese people from voting; voters finally removed the exclusion section in 1926.
government.kid_line: "The powers of the Government shall be divided into three separate branches" (Oregon Constitution, Article III, Section 1)

long_ago.nation: Earliest Oregonians (Fort Rock Cave and Paisley Caves)
long_ago.about: Caves in Lake County hold the oldest evidence of people in Oregon; material from Fort Rock Cave is about 13,200 years old.

long_ago.nation: Chinookan peoples (including the Clatsop, Wasco, and Wishram)
long_ago.about: Along the lower Columbia River, salmon was the main food, and families of 50 or more relatives shared long plankhouses built from red cedar. In the 1700s the Wishram village was the center of a trade network reaching the coast, the Plateau, the Great Basin, and the Plains.

Eight Kalapuya groups lived in the Willamette Valley. Women dug camas bulbs with digging sticks and gathered acorns, and each late autumn the people set careful fires on the prairies to enrich the soil and clear brush.

The Wallowa Band of the Nimíipuu, meaning "we, the people," lived in northeastern Oregon. They fished for Chinook salmon, dug camas and kouse roots (more than half of their food), and became famous horse breeders.

The Cayuse lived in northeastern Oregon and southeastern Washington in summer and winter river villages. They bred fast, strong horses, still called Cayuse ponies, and fished for salmon and gathered camas.
Klamath people kept alive the memory of the eruption of Mount Mazama about 7,700 years ago in a story of a battle between Llao and Skell that destroyed Llao's mountain home, where Crater Lake is now.

today.about: Federally recognized; mostly descendants of the Wadatika band of Northern Paiute, with a reservation north of Burns in Harney County, eastern Oregon.

today.nation: Confederated Tribes of the Coos, Lower Umpqua and Siuslaw Indians
today.about: Federally recognized; three tribes and four bands (Hanis Coos, Miluk Coos, Lower Umpqua, and Siuslaw) from the central and southern Oregon coast.

today.nation: Confederated Tribes of the Grand Ronde Community of Oregon
today.about: Federally recognized; more than 30 tribes and bands, including Kalapuya, Molalla, Chasta, Umpqua, Rogue River, Chinook, and Tillamook, with a reservation in Yamhill County. The U.S. ended its recognition in 1954 and restored it in 1983.

today.nation: Confederated Tribes of Siletz Indians of Oregon
today.about: Federally recognized; a confederation of 27 bands with a reservation in Lincoln County. Termination was forced on them in 1955, and in November 1977 they became the first Oregon tribe restored to federal recognition.

today.nation: Confederated Tribes of the Umatilla Indian Reservation
today.about: Federally recognized; the Cayuse, Umatilla, and Walla Walla peoples, with a reservation near Pendleton in northeastern Oregon kept under an 1855 treaty.

today.nation: Confederated Tribes of the Warm Springs Reservation of Oregon
today.about: Federally recognized; the Warm Springs, Wasco, and Paiute peoples, whose reservation stretches from the Cascade Mountains to the Deschutes River in central Oregon.
Federally recognized; descendants of people of the Coquille River watershed and lower Coos Bay, whose federal recognition was restored in 1989.

today.nation: Cow Creek Band of Umpqua Tribe of Indians
today.about: Federally recognized; based in Roseburg in southwestern Oregon. The tribe never received the reservation its treaty promised, but its people stayed in their homelands.
Federally recognized; the Klamath, Modoc, and Yahooskin peoples, centered in Klamath County near Chiloquin and Klamath Falls.

first_peoples.today_note: Oregon has nine federally recognized tribes today. After the 1850 Donation Land Claim Act gave Native lands to white settlers before any treaties were made, many nations were forced onto reservations, and several, including Siletz, Grand Ronde, and Coquille, lost federal recognition in the 1950s and later fought to win it back.
sites: Crater Lake National Park, the lake left by Mount Mazama's eruption, remembered in Klamath stories
Fort Clatsop, where the Lewis and Clark expedition spent the winter of 1805 to 1806
Nez Perce Wallowa Homeland, a 320-acre site with a visitor center at Wallowa
Fort Rock Cave and Paisley Caves (Lake County), the oldest known places people lived in Oregon

history.event: People live at Fort Rock Cave in what is now Lake County, the oldest known evidence of people in Oregon.
Mount Mazama erupts and collapses; its caldera fills with water to become Crater Lake. Klamath people keep the event alive in their stories.

The Lewis and Clark expedition reaches the Pacific. On November 24, 1805, the group votes on where to spend the winter; York, an enslaved Black man, and Sacagawea both vote. They build Fort Clatsop and leave on March 23, 1806.
Fort Astoria, paid for by John Jacob Astor, becomes the first lasting European American settlement in Oregon.
John McLoughlin runs the Hudson's Bay Company fur trade from Fort Vancouver. Meanwhile, diseases brought by newcomers kill most of the Kalapuya, who may have numbered 15,000 before contact.
The Great Migration: about 700 to 1,000 people travel the Oregon Trail to the Willamette Valley. About 400,000 people will use the trail and its branches.

On June 26, Oregon's Provisional Government passes its first Black exclusion law, ordering Black settlers to leave or be whipped; that part was soon replaced and the law was repealed in 1845. The same year, Robin and Polly Holmes are brought west, enslaved, by Nathaniel Ford.
After a measles epidemic kills many Cayuse people, Cayuse men attack the Whitman Mission on November 29, 1847. Congress creates Oregon Territory on August 14, 1848.

A second exclusion law bans Black people from moving to Oregon. The Donation Land Claim Act of 1850 gives Native land to white settlers before treaties are signed, and the first Chinese immigrants arrive.
On July 13, the Oregon Territorial Supreme Court rules in Holmes v. Ford that Robin and Polly Holmes's children must be returned to their free parents.

Treaties force nations to give up most of their land: the Cayuse, Umatilla, and Walla Walla keep the Umatilla Reservation, the Wasco and Warm Springs peoples keep the Warm Springs Reservation, and many western Oregon peoples are moved to Grand Ronde.
Voters reject slavery (7,727 to 2,645) but approve keeping free Black people out of Oregon (8,640 to 1,081). In the same November vote they approve the state constitution.
Oregon becomes the 33rd state on February 14.

During the Civil War, regular U.S. soldiers leave to fight for the Union, and the First Oregon Cavalry keeps watch at home until June 1865. In 1862 the state taxes Black, Chinese, and Hawaiian residents $5 each.
Chief Joseph and about 750 Nimíipuu (Nez Perce) begin a 1,170-mile flight from U.S. soldiers on June 15 and surrender in Montana on October 5.

trailblazers.name: York
trailblazers.text: York was enslaved by William Clark and helped the Lewis and Clark expedition hunt and haul boats to the Pacific. At the mouth of the Columbia in 1805 he voted with the rest of the group on where to camp for the winter, but after the trip he got no pay or land, and Clark did not free him.

trailblazers.name: Robin and Polly Holmes
trailblazers.text: Robin and Polly Holmes were brought to Oregon in 1844 by their enslaver, Nathaniel Ford, who freed them in 1850 but kept four of their children. Robin sued in 1852, and in 1853 the territorial supreme court returned the children to their parents, a key legal challenge to slavery in Oregon.

trailblazers.name: Abner Hunt Francis and Sydna Francis
trailblazers.text: Abner Francis, an abolitionist who had worked with Frederick Douglass in Buffalo, New York, and his wife Sydna, an activist for abolition and women's voting rights, came to Portland in 1851, where Abner ran a store whose property was worth about $36,000 by 1860. When officials tried to force the family out under the exclusion law, more than 200 residents signed a petition for them and they stayed; in 1865, in Victoria, Canada, Abner became the first Black person elected to that city's council.

trailblazers.name: John McLoughlin
trailblazers.text: As chief of the Hudson's Bay Company at Fort Vancouver, McLoughlin went against company orders to help American wagon trains in the early 1840s, and Oregon's legislature named him the "Father of Oregon" in 1957. He was known for fair dealing, but a company ship under his command also attacked a S'Klallam village and killed 27 people.

trailblazers.name: Chief Joseph (Young Joseph)
trailblazers.text: Chief Joseph was a leader of the Wallowa Band from northeastern Oregon. In 1877 he helped lead about 750 people on a long flight from the U.S. Army, and at his surrender he said, "From where the sun now stands, I will fight no more forever." In 1879 he went to Washington, D.C., to speak for his people.

trailblazers.name: Abigail Scott Duniway
trailblazers.text: Abigail Scott Duniway came to Oregon by wagon in 1852 and founded the New Northwest newspaper in Portland in 1871 to fight for women's rights. When Oregon men voted for woman suffrage in 1912, she was asked to write the official proclamation and sign it with the governor, and she became the first Oregon woman to register to vote.

trailblazers.name: Gladys Thompson
trailblazers.text: Gladys Thompson was the last fully fluent speaker of Kiksht, the Upper Chinook language of the Wasco people at Warm Springs. Her life reminds students why tribes today work hard to keep their languages alive.

waters: Columbia River (much of the northern border)
Crater Lake (deepest lake in the U.S.)
geography.regions: Oregon has a rainy Pacific coast, the fertile Willamette Valley where about 60% of Oregonians live, the volcanic Cascade Range, and high desert covering much of the eastern two-thirds of the state.

ecosystems.name: Columbia River salmon country
ecosystems.about: Chinook salmon, the state fish, were the main food of the Chinookan peoples and a staple and ceremony for the Nimíipuu.

ecosystems.name: Willamette Valley prairies
ecosystems.about: The Kalapuya used autumn fires to keep the valley's grass prairies open, which encouraged many kinds of plants and animals; the valley's rich soil came from the ancient Missoula Floods.

ecosystems.name: Douglas-fir forests
ecosystems.about: The Douglas-fir is the state tree, and Oregon is the top lumber producer in the lower 48 states, though forest fires such as the Tillamook Burn and over-cutting have changed the forests.

ecosystems.name: High desert
ecosystems.about: Dry high desert covers much of eastern Oregon; the state's coldest temperature, minus 54°F, was recorded at Seneca on February 10, 1933.

science.weather: Western Oregon has wet winters and dry summers, while the east is dry steppe and high mountains are colder. The state faces earthquake and tsunami danger from the Juan de Fuca Plate (the last great quake was the 1700 Cascadia earthquake), volcanoes in the Cascades (Mount St. Helens' 1980 eruption affected northern Oregon), and forest fires.
science.resources: Oregon's economy grew from farming, fishing, logging, and hydroelectric power from its rivers; it is still the top lumber producer in the lower 48 states and has a large technology industry called the "Silicon Forest."
science.highlight: Crater Lake: about 7,700 years ago the volcano Mount Mazama erupted and collapsed, leaving a bowl that filled with rain and snow. At 1,949 feet deep it is the deepest lake in the United States, and the park gets about 463 inches of snow a year.

g3_ss.title: Oregon's Communities and Government
g3_ss.plan: Map Salem, Portland, and the student's town; learn the Legislative Assembly (Senate 30, House 60), the governor, and the Supreme Court; talk about Article III, Section 1 and the three branches.

g3_ss.title: Oregon's First Peoples
g3_ss.plan: Meet the Chinookan peoples, Kalapuya, Nimíipuu, Cayuse, and Klamath; build a model cedar plankhouse; find Oregon's nine federally recognized tribes on a map today.

g3_ss.title: Oregon Trailblazers
g3_ss.plan: Timeline cards for York, Robin and Polly Holmes, Abner and Sydna Francis, Chief Joseph, Abigail Scott Duniway, and Gladys Thompson; students write how each one stood up for freedom, voting rights, language, or home.

g45_ss.title: Oregon's First Nations
g45_ss.plan: Fort Rock Cave, Mount Mazama in Klamath memory, salmon and plankhouse life on the Columbia, Wishram trade, camas and fire on Kalapuya prairies, and horse cultures of the Plateau.

g45_ss.title: Explorers, Fur Traders, and the Oregon Trail
g45_ss.plan: Lewis and Clark's winter (and York's and Sacagawea's votes), Fort Astoria, McLoughlin and Fort Vancouver, disease among the Kalapuya, and the 1843 Great Migration.

g45_ss.title: Oregon 1844–1877
g45_ss.plan: Exclusion laws and the Holmes v. Ford case, the 1847 Whitman attack and Oregon Territory, the Donation Land Claim Act and 1855 treaties, the 1857 votes, statehood in 1859, the Civil War years, and the 1877 Nez Perce flight.

g3_sci.title: Salmon Journey
g3_sci.plan: Life cycle of the Chinook salmon from river to ocean and back; why rivers and clean water matter to people and animals.

g3_sci.title: Forests and Beavers
g3_sci.plan: Douglas-fir forests, the beaver as a builder of ponds, and how forests grow back after fire.

g3_sci.title: Oregon Weather Watch
g3_sci.plan: Compare rainy western Oregon with the dry high desert using real temperature and rain records; keep a weather journal.

g45_sci.title: Volcano to Lake: Crater Lake
g45_sci.plan: How Mount Mazama erupted and collapsed into a caldera, why the lake is so deep and clear, and how Klamath stories record the event.

g45_sci.title: Living on a Moving Plate
g45_sci.plan: The Juan de Fuca Plate, the 1700 Cascadia earthquake, tsunami safety, and Cascade volcanoes such as Mount Hood and Mount St. Helens.

g45_sci.title: Floods, Soil, and Farms
g45_sci.plan: How the Missoula Floods built Willamette Valley soil, how Kalapuya fire kept prairies healthy, and how farms use that soil today.
